publication_scope.blurb: Ludwig Crocius — Book I Chapter 9 On Sacred Scripture's parts, from the 1636 Bremen Latin. Densify COMPLETE (PHYS 290–mid-302): partes defined as canonical OT/NT books; duplex criterion (internal inspiration and external catholic testimony); four inferences on canonical authority, one canon reason, judging controversies, and scriptural sufficiency against unwritten word; OT historical/poetic/prophetic classes; Apocrypha; NT four integral parts (evangelical, practical, epistolary, apocalyptic). Cap. 10 begins PHYS 302; Cap. 8 complete; the rest of the Syntagma remains.

source_text: CAPUT NONUM. De sacrae Scripturae partibus. Hactenus Scripturae sacrae affectiones fuerunt: sequuntur partes, nimirum libri canonici Veteris ac Novi Testamenti ab hominibus Spiritu Dei sancto afflatis & directis scripti & approbati ad authentice declarandam universam, quae quidem ad religionem pertinet, Dei voluntatem. Canonici quasi legitimi & regulares dicuntur a canone, cujus rex David ps. 19.v.8. & Apostolus Gal. 1.v.6.7.8.9. & 6.v.16. Phil. 3.v.15.16. commemorat, qui ab iis hominibus qui a Spiritu S. afflati ac directi fuerunt, in hoc scripti aut approbati sunt, ut fidei vitaeque norma & mensura sint perpetua secundum utriusque Testamenti statum & conditionem, 2. Tim. 3.v.15.16. 2. Pet. 1.v.20.21. & opponuntur Apocryphis, id est, omnibus iis, qui fidem Christianam non regunt & metiuntur. Nam & Apocryphi quidam his in bibliis adjunguntur akavonistoi irregulares, qui ob lectionis utilitatem, non ob certam suam divinitatem nonnunquam deuterocanonici & Ecclesiastici a priscis dicti, ad sacrae Scripturae partes nonnisi improprie referri possunt, de quibus infra aph. 13. 14. & 15. Canonici libri dicuntur & apodechomenoi in confesso existentes, euapodektoi testamentarii & a S. Athanasio ta kanonizomena biblia, libri in canonem recepti, ut est in variis lectionibus H. Savilii ad vitam S. Antonii ab Heschelio editis. Duplex autem momentum est & kriterion, e quo judicium fit de unoquoque scripto sacro, quod sit canonicum accurate & specialiter dictum, internum & externum.
english:
CHAPTER NINE
On Sacred Scripture's parts

So far the affections of Sacred Scripture have been treated: the parts follow — namely the canonical books of the Old and New Testament, written and approved by men inspired and directed by God's Holy Spirit, for authentically declaring the whole will of God that pertains to religion.

They are called canonical as legitimate and regular from the canon of which king David ([[Psalm 19:8 >> Bible:Psalm 19:8]]) and the Apostle ([[Galatians 1:6 >> Bible:Galatians 1:6]]-[[Galatians 1:9 >> Bible:Galatians 1:9]]; [[Galatians 6:16 >> Bible:Galatians 6:16]]; [[Philippians 3:15 >> Bible:Philippians 3:15]]-[[Philippians 3:16 >> Bible:Philippians 3:16]]) make mention — books which by those men who were inspired and directed by the Holy Spirit were written or approved for this, that they might be a perpetual norm and measure of faith and life according to the state and condition of each Testament ([[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]-[[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]; [[2 Peter 1:20 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:20]]-[[2 Peter 1:21 >> Bible:2 Peter 1:21]]), and they are opposed to the Apocrypha, that is, to all those that do not rule and measure the Christian faith.

For certain Apocrypha are also joined to these in the Bibles — irregulars — which for the usefulness of reading, not for their certain divinity, were sometimes called deuterocanonical and Ecclesiastical by the ancients, and can be referred to Sacred Scripture's parts only improperly, of which below at Aph. 13, 14, and 15. Canonical books are also called books existing by confession, testamentary, and by St. Athanasius books received into the canon, as in the variant readings of H. Savile on the Life of St. Antony edited by Heschel. And there is a double criterion from which judgment is made concerning each sacred writing that it is canonical accurately and specially so called — internal and external.

source_text: XXIII. Superest Apocalyptica, quarta pars N.T., a Johanne Apostolo conscripta de iis, quae Christus ipse revelavit de statu ecclesiarum novi testamenti, ab illius initio per septem distinctas periodos & facies in Ephesina, Smyrnenfi, Pergamenfi, Thyatirenfi, Sardenfi, Philadelphenfi & Laodicena effigiatas usque ad finem mundi, deque earum donis, periculis, calamitatibus, Antichristi persecutionibus, liberationibus, extremo judicio, impiorum horrenda damnatione, ecclesiarum piorumque in ea summa glorificatione, ne fatorum suorum sortisque futurae ignari, instar gentilium aut brutorum, subitaneis casibus obruerentur ac perirent, sed eventuum praedictorum experimento paulatim docti agnoscerent, se Christo semper curae esse.
english: XXIII. There remains the Apocalyptic, the fourth part of the New Testament, written by the Apostle John concerning those things which Christ himself revealed about the state of the New Testament churches — from its beginning through seven distinct periods and faces portrayed in the Ephesian, Smyrnaean, Pergamene, Thyatiran, Sardian, Philadelphian, and Laodicean, unto the world's end — and concerning their gifts, dangers, calamities, Antichrist's persecutions, deliverances, the last judgment, the dreadful damnation of the impious, and the supreme glorification of the churches and the godly in it — lest, ignorant of their own fates and future lot, like Gentiles or brute beasts, they should be overwhelmed and perish by sudden chances; but taught little by little by the experience of predicted events, they might acknowledge that they are always Christ's care.

source_text: 3. Omnes libros canonicos posse judicare & determinare controversias religionis. Haec enim est canonis vis, 2. Tim. 3.v.15.16. psal. 119.v.9. Rom. 2.v.16. Heb. 4.v.12. Joh. 3.v.18. & 12.v.48. Joh. 16.v.8. Judicat autem ac determinat sacra Scriptura kanonikos, per modum regulae, spiritus sanctus in ea loquens, pistos, per modum authentiae, Ecclesia diakoniikos, per modum ministrae, praeses vero in illa hic aut ille cum assessoribus suis mesikos, per modum personae, cui id accidit, qui si sit judex adekastos, unum idemque horum omnium, adeoque divinum & infallibile fiet judicium, de quo rectius docet inter philosophos nostros Cornelius Martinius Analysis parte 2. cap. 3. quam Bellarminus lib. 3. de V.D. cap. 9. 4. Canonis sacri autarkeian & fidei moribusque Christianis adaequatam sufficientiam, qua omnia creditu factuque Christianis necessaria debito modo in eo contineantur, ut hodie, postquam verbum Dei literis consignatum & Ecclesiae creditum fuit, aliud verbum Dei non scriptum, vel non in Bibliis scriptum, sed ab Apostolis in modum Cabbalae profectum, ad salutem, aliisque dogmatibus fidei in Bibliis neque quod ad literam, neque quod ad sensum exstantibus stabiliendis necessarium pari pietatis affectu cum verbo Dei scripto excipere nullo modo teneamur. Hoc enim, tum nomen canonis, quo Scriptura insignitur psal. 19.v.5. Gal. 6.v.16. tum res ipsa docet, psal. 19.v.8. 2. Tim. 3.v.15.16. Jacob. 1.v.21. Joh. 20.v.31. & 5.v.39. 1. Cor. 4.v.6. Gal. 1.v.8. Contra sophisticam imperfectionis criminationem Joh. Fischeri Roffensis Episcopi in confut. art. 27. col. 585. Jo. Eccii in enchir. L.C. q. 4. fol. 33. Conr. Klingii lib. 3. L.C. cap. 3. p. 194. Wilhelmi Lindani lib. 1. panopl. Euang. cap. 22. p. 33. Melior. Cani lib. 3. Locor. Theol. cap. 3. Mart. Peresii lib. de tradit. part. 2. fol. 28.30. Renati Benedicti in panoplia Catholicorum p. 595. Alphonsi a Castro lib. 1. adv. haereses cap. 1. Franc. Agricolae de verbo Dei scripto & non scripto cap. 9. p. 66. Greg. de Valentia lib. 5. Analy. fidei catholicae cap. 3. & lib. 8. Anal. cap. 6. p. 102. Rob. Bellarmin. lib. 4. de V.D. cap. 3. Franc. Costeri ench. controvers. cap. 1. p. 44.45. Thom. Stapletoni prompt. cathol. Dom. Sexag. p. 83. Henrici Lancelloti in haeretico Quare, q. 18. p. 172. & Anatom. Christiani deformati p. 33. Viti Mileti in brevi discussione 600. errorum Hesbusii ref. error. 2. p. 8. & err. 3. p. 11. Adami Tanneri in colloq. Ratisp. sess. 12. p. 355. Jacobi Gordoni Huntlaei tom. 1. epit. controv. 1. c. 27. p. 125. & cap. 32. p. 140.142. & cap. 33. p. 144. Mart. Becani lib. 1. Man. cap. 2. pag. 32. usque ad pag. 53. Contra quos pseudoprophetas, totumque suum examen pontificium lege succincte eruditeque disserentem de libris canonicis & Apocryphis doctissimum D. Antonium Thysium, Theologum Leidensem, Synopsis purioris Theologiae disp. 3. cum aliis ibi a nobis laudatis.
english: (3) That all canonical books can judge and determine controversies of religion. For this is the canon's force ([[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]-[[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]; [[Psalm 119:9 >> Bible:Psalm 119:9]]; [[Romans 2:16 >> Bible:Romans 2:16]]; [[Hebrews 4:12 >> Bible:Hebrews 4:12]]; [[John 3:18 >> Bible:John 3:18]]; [[John 12:48 >> Bible:John 12:48]]; [[John 16:8 >> Bible:John 16:8]]). And Sacred Scripture judges and determines by way of a rule; the Holy Spirit speaking in it, by way of authenticity; the Church by way of a minister; and the president in it — this one or that with his assessors — by way of the person to whom it falls; who if he is an uncorrupted judge, the judgment of all these becomes one and the same, and so divine and infallible — on which Cornelius Martinius among our philosophers teaches more rightly in Analysis part 2 chapter 3 than Bellarmine in On the Word of God book 3 chapter 9.

(4) The sacred canon's self-sufficiency and its adequate sufficiency for Christian faith and manners — by which all things necessary for Christians to believe and do are contained in it in due manner — so that today, after God's word has been committed to letters and entrusted to the Church, we are in no way bound to receive with equal pious affection, together with the written word of God, another unwritten word of God, or one not written in the Bibles but handed down from the Apostles in Cabbalah-fashion, as necessary for salvation and for establishing other dogmas of faith that stand in the Bibles neither as to letter nor as to sense. For both the name "canon" by which Scripture is marked ([[Psalm 19:5 >> Bible:Psalm 19:5]]; [[Galatians 6:16 >> Bible:Galatians 6:16]]) and the thing itself teach this ([[Psalm 19:8 >> Bible:Psalm 19:8]]; [[2 Timothy 3:15 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:15]]-[[2 Timothy 3:16 >> Bible:2 Timothy 3:16]]; [[James 1:21 >> Bible:James 1:21]]; [[John 20:31 >> Bible:John 20:31]]; [[John 5:39 >> Bible:John 5:39]]; [[1 Corinthians 4:6 >> Bible:1 Corinthians 4:6]]; [[Galatians 1:8 >> Bible:Galatians 1:8]]).

Against the sophistic charge of imperfection from John Fisher Bishop of Rochester, John Eck, Conrad Kling, Wilhelm Lindanus, Melchior Cano, Martin Perez de Ayala, Rene Benoist, Alphonsus de Castro, Franz Agricola, Gregory of Valencia, Robert Bellarmine, Francis Coster, Thomas Stapleton, Heinrich Lancellot, Vitus Miletus, Adam Tanner, James Gordon Huntly, and Martin Becanus — against which false prophets and their whole papal examination read the most learned Dr. Antonius Thysius, Leiden theologian, succinctly and learnedly treating of canonical and Apocryphal books in Synopsis of Purer Theology Disputation 3, with others praised there by us.

source_text: V. Pentateuchus continet Genesin, Exodum, Leviticum, Numeros, Deuteronomium: de quibus vide Theologiam contractam lib. 1. c. 9. aph. 6.7.8.9.10. VI. Triteuchus tres libros, nempe Josue, Judicum & Ruth complectitur. Vide ibidem Aph. 11.12.13. VII. Octateuchus est, qui continet octo sequentes libros, duos Samuelis, Regum duos, duos Chronicorum, librum Esrae & Nehemiae, librumque Estherae. vide ibidem aph. 14.15. & seqq. usque ad 23. VIII. Et hi sunt libri historici antiqui Hebraeorum canonis: Sequentur poetici, qui sunt elegantissima legis prophetarumque praxis et epitome, ut Jobus, Psalmi, Proverbia, Ecclesiastes, Canticum canticorum. Vide ibidem c. 11. de libris poeticis totum.
english: V. The Pentateuch contains Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy — on which see Contracted Theology book 1 chapter 9 Aph. 6-10.
VI. The Triteuch embraces three books, namely Joshua, Judges, and Ruth. See there Aph. 11-13.

VII. The Octateuch is that which contains the eight following books: the two of Samuel, the two of Kings, the two of Chronicles, the book of Ezra and Nehemiah, and the book of Esther. See there Aph. 14-15 and following through 23.

VIII. And these are the historical books of the ancient Hebrew canon. The poetic follow, which are the most elegant practice and epitome of the law and the prophets — as Job, the Psalms, Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Song of Songs. See there chapter 11 on the poetic books entire.

source_text: XVI. Et hucusque fuerunt etiam Apocryphi: Sequuntur libri Canonici N.T. qui sunt tabulae sacrosancti contractus inter Deum & genus humanum, agni Dei jam mactati sanguine constabiliti, conscriptae ab octo amanuensibus, viris optimis, testibus omni exceptione majoribus, a Spiritu sancto afflatis. XVII. Partes vero N.T. integrales sunt quatuor: una Euangelica, altera practica, tertia epistolica, quarta denique Apocalyptica. XVIII. Euangelica pars a quatuor Euangelistis, Matthaeo, Marco, Luca, & Johanne de conceptione, nativitate, doctrina, vita, mirandis operibus, passione, morte, abitu ad patrem, redituque Jesu Nazareni, magno in re consensu conscripta est ad demonstrandum, hunc esse promissum Messiam.
english: XVI. And thus far the Apocrypha also. There follow the canonical books of the New Testament, which are the tables of the most holy contract between God and the human race, established by the blood of the Lamb of God already slain — written by eight amanuenses, excellent men, witnesses beyond all exception, inspired by the Holy Spirit.
XVII. And the integral parts of the New Testament are four: one Evangelical, another practical, a third epistolary, and finally a fourth Apocalyptic.

XVIII. The Evangelical part was written by the four Evangelists — Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John — concerning the conception, birth, teaching, life, wonderful works, passion, death, departure to the Father, and return of Jesus of Nazareth, with great agreement in the matter, to demonstrate that this one is the promised Messiah.
